description: We’re a team of friends who met in college and graduated in Software Engineering. Our interests and skills span most areas of STEM. We chose to take on the “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars” challenge because we saw it as a chance to put our knowledge to the test and learn something new along the way.
summary:
SLOPE (Systematic Lunar and Planetary Analog Evaluation) is a data-driven project designed to identify Earth locations that can serve as analogs for potential permanent lunar bases and Mars exploration sites. 

The project develops an automated geospatial pipeline that collects, processes, and compares open datasets from NASA and other space agencies, evaluating environmental and terrain characteristics across Earth, the Moon, and Mars. It considers key mission requirements such as solar illumination, water and ice availability, subsurface shelter potential, terrain mobility, and landing safety.
By combining multiple scientific criteria into quantitative similarity assessments and rankings, SLOPE moves beyond visual comparisons and the traditional reliance on a small number of well-known analog sites. It identifies locations that may reproduce specific planetary conditions, while recognizing that no single Earth location can replicate every aspect of an extraterrestrial environment.

SLOPE aims to support researchers, mission planners, and engineers in selecting terrestrial testing and training sites, reducing uncertainty, improving technology validation, and helping prepare for the challenges of sustained human exploration beyond Earth.
details:
Link for project: https://novo-oeste-nasa-slope.streamlit.app/

SLOPE (Systematic Lunar and Planetary Analog Evaluation) is a geospatial analysis tool designed to systematically identify terrestrial locations that resemble potential lunar exploration and settlement sites.

The project works through an automated data-processing pipeline that collects, processes, and compares planetary and Earth elevation datasets. It currently analyzes two lunar reference locations, Shackleton and Haworth craters, against six predefined terrestrial candidates: the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley, Pinacate, Tolbachik, and Meteor Crater.

Using NASA's LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) elevation data and lunar solar illumination datasets, alongside Copernicus Digital Elevation Models, SLOPE calculates terrain characteristics at a common 120-meter analysis spacing. It evaluates three primary dimensions: slope distribution, terrain roughness at multiple spatial scales, and local elevation relief. Statistical distance metrics, including the Wasserstein distance, are combined into weighted similarity rankings. Sensitivity analyses test how different criteria weights affect the results.

The main benefit is providing a reproducible, quantitative alternative to selecting analog sites based primarily on visual resemblance or a limited number of traditionally recognized locations. Its intended impact is to help researchers, engineers, and mission planners identify promising terrestrial environments for testing exploration technologies, preparing astronauts, and studying terrain-related operational challenges before deploying missions beyond Earth.

The project was developed primarily in Python, using NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, PyProj, Pandas, Matplotlib, and Requests for numerical analysis, geospatial processing, statistical comparisons, data acquisition, and visualization. It uses open scientific datasets and does not require specialized hardware.

SLOPE's creative approach lies in transforming planetary terrain data into comparable mathematical signatures and evaluating analog suitability through multiple independent criteria rather than a single similarity score. It also incorporates ranking sensitivity analysis and data-quality checks to identify potential biases and limitations.

The team considered terrain morphology, slope constraints, surface roughness, elevation variability, spatial resolution, data quality, and the limitations of comparing measurements collected by different instruments on different planetary bodies.

Ultimately, SLOPE aims to make planetary exploration preparation more systematic, transparent, reproducible, and accessible through open data and computational science.
